With a fermentation crock, it's crazy easy.

  • Shred a medium head of cabbage per L of size of your crock (5l crock, up to five heads.)
  • As you shred each head, beat the hell out of it with a stick or your gloved hands, along with 1-2 tbs of salt (per head). I like pickling salt because it dissolves faster, but use something without iodine added. Vegetables already have enough iodine, and in something with lots of salt, iodine tastes funny. You will know if you are really smashing it down because it will give off a lot of liquid. When you have smashed it enough, it will be like cabbage soup.
  • Put the smashed cabbage and juice in the crock, smash it down as much as you can with your bare hands (some of the lactobacillus that you want will come from your skin -- the gloves earlier was to keep you from tearing your hands up with all the smashing) so that the cabbage is submerged in the juice, and then put your weights (the little half-moons) on top of that in a ring. If the weights aren't covered, you didn't smash enough, so get a stick or spoon or something and really put a thrashing on it.
  • Put the lid on and put water in the airlock ring. (Our cat kept drinking the water up, so we put a tiny bit of vinegar in it to keep her away.)
  • STOP TOUCHING IT. Seriously. Leave it alone for at least two weeks. If you keep your place cold, it will take longer, up to four weeks. If the water gets low, jiggle the lid a little without lifting it, because sometimes the barometric pressure pushes the water in. If it is still low after jiggling, top it off. Just don't take the lid off.
  • When it stops bubbling, it is done. Don't check it and then recover it. Once you've opened it, you're committed. That's why you want to be sure that you sit there reading a book or something in quiet for at least five minutes and make sure it doesn't burp.

Eat it cold, fry it with apples and onions (lightly, the bacteria in it are good for your biome), or freeze it. It will keep for a few weeks in the fridge or for who knows how long in the freezer. If you can it, the canning process kills the bacteria, (because, duh, that's what canning is for) and you lose some of the probiotic effects. It will keep forever that way, though, if you just want the calories and fiber.

Making it yourself is really the only way to get the probiotic effects. Commercial kraut is always pasteurized, so the bacteria are always dead.

  • One more thing -- if you don't want to invest in a crock right away, or if you are single feeding yourself, you can also buy/make an airlock for mason jars, and do it that way. It might even be easier, since you can see the bubbling and see if you've got slime going. Don't put it in direct sunlight, though, because the UV will kill the bacteria.

Making dimsum style chicken feet is easy and delicious.

  • Cut the nails off. Soak in baking soda and salt solution for a couple hours.
  • Dry well.
  • Deep fry for a few minutes and drop into cold water.
  • Fry fermented black bean, sliced red chilis, garlic, and a small amount of star anise in a small amount of oil, mix into a solution of starch and water over medium heat to get it a little sticky like gravy.
  • Put chicken feet into metal bowl for steaming and pour over the spice gravy, let it cook about 20 minutes.

Since steaming is the final step it's easy to keep them on-hand for a few days in the fridge and just steam a batch when you want them.
